```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# The ragg device writes smaller figure files; without it the default is used.
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
options(bayesEfron.use_cli = FALSE, width = 80)
has_loo <- requireNamespace("loo", quietly = TRUE)
has_bayesplot <- requireNamespace("bayesplot", quietly = TRUE)
```

This vignette shows what each plot function in bayesEfron is for and how
to read the result. A fit contains a posterior distribution for $g$, the
distribution of effects, and for the effect of every site, and most
questions about it are easier to answer from a plot than from a table.

```{r library}
library(bayesEfron)
```

Each plot function returns a `ggplot` object that you can change with
ggplot2 functions. The one exception is `plot_mcmc(type = "pairs")`,
which returns the grid of plots that bayesplot makes.

For most examples we use two fits stored in the package: `krw_fit`, the
callback gaps of 97 firms from `vignette("bayesEfron")`, and
`twin_towers_fit`, 1,500 simulated sites with known true effects from
`vignette("twin-towers")`.

```{r fits}
firms <- krw_fit
sims <- twin_towers_fit
truth <- twin_towers$theta_true
```

## The distribution of effects

`plot_g()` shows what the distribution of true effects looks like and how
well the data determine it. The curve is the posterior mean of the
density of $g$, and the pointwise band around it contains the density
with the stated probability at each value. Below, `observed` puts a
histogram of the estimates under the curve, `normal` puts a normal
distribution fitted to the same estimates over it, and `scale = 100`
gives percentage points.

```{r g, fig.alt = "The estimated density of the callback gaps with its band, a histogram of the estimates and a dashed normal curve."}
plot_g(firms, observed = "histogram", normal = TRUE, scale = 100)
```

The histogram is wider than the curve because the estimates contain
sampling error and the effects do not. Where the band is wide, the data
do not determine the height of the density well.

Proportions of sites are easier to read from the distribution function,
so next we set `type = "cdf"`. Setting `inner_level` adds a second,
narrower band.

```{r g-cdf, fig.alt = "The estimated distribution function of the callback gaps with a 50 percent band inside a 90 percent band."}
plot_g(firms, type = "cdf", inner_level = 0.5, scale = 100)
```

The height of the curve at a value is the proportion of firms with a gap
below it. Three more arguments add to the plot:

- `draws = 40` adds 40 posterior draws of $g$ to its posterior mean and
  band.
- `truth` adds the true effects of simulated data.
- `compare` puts other estimates of the distribution over this one, from
  other fits or from other software.

## The sites

### Caterpillar plot

A caterpillar plot from `plot_sites()` shows the posterior mean of each
site with a 50% and a 90% interval, and the estimate as an open circle.
Use it to see which sites have the largest and the smallest effects, and
how certain that ordering is.

```{r sites, fig.height = 5.2, fig.alt = "Two panels with the ten firms with the highest and the ten with the lowest posterior mean gaps, by name."}
plot_sites(firms, n_extreme = 10, scale = 100)
```

`n_extreme` selects the sites at the two ends, and `sites` selects sites
by name or position. Without either, every site is plotted: labeled when
there are at most 100, and as thin lines when there are more.

```{r sites-many, message = FALSE, fig.alt = "The 90 percent intervals of the 1,500 simulated sites as thin lines in the order of the posterior means."}
plot_sites(sims)
```

### Shrinkage plot

`plot_shrinkage()` shows how far the model moves the estimates by
plotting the posterior mean of every site against its estimate. Points on
the diagonal have not moved.

```{r shrinkage, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "The posterior mean of each firm against its estimate, colored by standard error."}
plot_shrinkage(firms, scale = 100)
```

With `style = "arrows"`, each site is an arrow from the estimate to the
posterior mean, at the height of its standard error. This suits a small
number of sites, such as the 19 teacher expectancy studies in the stored
fit `raudenbush_fit`.

```{r shrinkage-arrows, fig.alt = "For each of the 19 teacher expectancy studies an arrow from the estimate to the posterior mean, at the height of its standard error."}
plot_shrinkage(raudenbush_fit, style = "arrows")
```

### Exceedance probabilities

When the question is which sites have an effect above a threshold,
`plot_exceedance()` plots, for each site, the posterior probability that
its effect is above the threshold. `cutoff` marks a probability and counts the sites that reach it.
For many sites, the probabilities are plotted as a curve.

```{r exceedance, message = FALSE, fig.alt = "The probabilities that the effects of the 1,500 simulated sites are positive, in increasing order, with a dashed line at 0.9."}
plot_exceedance(sims, cutoff = 0.9)
```

The caption notes that the count controls no error rate over the sites,
which is easy to forget when a list of sites is made from it.

### The posterior of one site

`plot_site_posterior()` plots the whole posterior distribution of a site,
with the two things that it is made from: the likelihood of the estimate
and the estimate of $g$.

```{r site-posterior, fig.height = 4.6, fig.alt = "Two panels: an imprecise site between the two groups, whose posterior distribution has two modes, and the most precise site, whose posterior distribution is narrow."}
plot_site_posterior(sims, sites = c(268, 304))
```

The first site has an imprecise estimate between the two groups of
simulated effects, and its posterior distribution has two modes. A mean
and an interval would hide that.

## Checking a fit

### Sampler and grid diagnostics

`plot_diagnostics()` plots what `diagnose()` reports, so you can check
two things at once: whether the sampler converged, and whether the grid
suits the fit. R-hat and the effective sample sizes of the quantities
that the sampler records are shown in blocks against their thresholds,
with two more panels about the grid.

```{r diagnostics, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.2, fig.alt = "Five panels: R-hat, bulk and tail effective sample sizes by block, the largest mass of a site at each end of the grid, and the standard deviation of the distribution of effects under the prior and the posterior."}
plot_diagnostics(firms)
```

Points to the right of the dashed line in the first panel (R-hat), or to
the left of it in the next two (effective sample sizes), would be
quantities that miss their thresholds. There are none here. The caption
gives the numbers of divergent transitions and
of iterations at the maximum tree depth, and `vignette("diagnostics")`
explains each check.

### Posterior predictive check

A posterior predictive check with `plot_ppc()` shows whether the model
reproduces the estimates. The check compares each estimate with the
distribution that the fitted model gives it, through the probability of a
smaller estimate at that site (the probability integral transform, PIT).
If $g$ were known, these values would be uniformly distributed between 0
and 1, and the line shows how far the values of the fitted model are from
that.

```{r ppc, fig.alt = "The empirical distribution function of the probability integral transforms of the 97 estimates less the uniform one, inside a gray band."}
plot_ppc(firms)
```

The band is the reference for independent uniform values, but it does not
allow for the fitting of $g$. See `vignette("diagnostics")` for how to
read it.

### Pareto k values

Leave-one-out cross-validation approximates the fit that would result
without each site, and the Pareto k of a site measures how good that
approximation is. To check that the approximation is reliable for every
site, plot the values with `plot_loo()`. A line marks the value above which the result
for a site should not be trusted, and the sites above it are labeled. See
`vignette("diagnostics")` for more.

```{r loo, eval = has_loo, fig.height = 3.2, fig.alt = "The Pareto k value of each of the 97 firms, all below the dashed line."}
plot_loo(firms)
```

## Grids and grid comparisons

The `plot()` method for a grid, or `plot(fit, type = "grid")` for the
grid of a fit, shows where the grid lies in relation to the data: the
spline functions, the knots and the grid points over the estimates.

```{r grid, fig.height = 4.6, fig.alt = "The eight spline basis functions and the knots of the grid of the simulated-site fit, over a histogram of the estimates."}
plot(sims, type = "grid")
```

The limits of this grid are well inside the range of the estimates
because the default `grid_method` narrowed it.

To see what changes when the grid changes, plot a comparison from
`compare_efron_grids()`: the specifications appear one under the other.
Here we load a stored comparison of three ranges for the 19 teacher
expectancy studies.

```{r comparison, fig.width = 8.5, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Three rows, one for each range of the grid for the 19 studies, each with the estimated density, the mean and standard deviation of the distribution, and the posterior means and intervals of two studies."}
comparison <- readRDS(system.file("examples", "raudenbush_ranges.rds",
                                  package = "bayesEfron"))
plot(comparison)
```

`vignette("twin-towers")` discusses the first of these plots and
`vignette("teacher-expectancy")` the second.

## Simulated data

With simulated data, `plot_recovery()` shows how close a fit comes to the
known effects. It plots the intervals of the sites with the true effects
and marks the sites where the true effect is outside. Only 150 sites are
shown, and `seed` fixes the random choice.

```{r recovery, fig.height = 4.8, fig.alt = "The 90 percent posterior intervals of 150 sites with their true effects as crosses, and as orange triangles where they lie outside the interval."}
plot_recovery(sims, truth, seed = 1)
```

Setting `type = "calibration"` shows the proportion of true effects
inside the intervals at every level from 5% to 95%, and
`type = "scatter"` plots the posterior means against the true effects.

## Common arguments

Every plot function takes the fit first, and a few arguments work the
same way wherever they apply:

- `scale` multiplies the effect values. For example, `scale = 100` turns
  differences in probabilities into percentage points.
- `level` sets the probability of posterior intervals and bands. In
  `plot_ppc()` it sets the level of the independent-uniform reference
  intervals.
- `sites` and `highlight` take positions or labels.

Calling `plot()` on a fit with a `type` runs the same functions by name,
so
`plot(firms, type = "g", scale = 100)` is the same as
`plot_g(firms, scale = 100)`.

## Customizing a plot

A plot has no title, but its caption says what the lines and bands are.
You can set both, and add layers, as with any other `ggplot` object:

```{r layers, fig.alt = "The density of the callback gaps with a title, an axis label and a vertical line at zero added."}
plot_g(firms, scale = 100) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Callback gaps of 97 firms",
                x = "White minus Black callback rate (percentage points)")
```

## Making your own plots

The numbers in the plots of $g$ and of the sites are also available from
three functions. The densities, distribution functions and probabilities of
$g$ come from `g_summary()`, the means and intervals of the sites from
`site_summary()`, and the probabilities of exceeding a threshold from
`exceedance_prob()`. To make a plot that the package does not have, start
from these functions:

```{r accessors}
head(g_summary(firms, type = "cdf", scale = 100), 3)
site_summary(firms, sites = c("KFC", "Walmart"), scale = 100)[, 1:8]
```

## MCMC plots with bayesplot

Trace plots, rank plots and the other plots of the Markov chains come
from bayesplot, and `plot_mcmc()` passes the draws of a fit to it. We
show a rank plot, in which the draws of all the chains are ranked
together and each line counts the ranks of one chain in 20 bins. Chains
that sample the same distribution give lines that overlap around a common
level, as they do here.

```{r mcmc, eval = has_bayesplot, fig.height = 2.6, fig.alt = "Rank plots of lambda and of the standard deviation of the distribution of effects: for each, four lines, one for each chain, that overlap around a common level."}
plot_mcmc(firms, type = "rank", pars = c("lambda", "sd_g"))
```

The `type` argument can be `"trace"`, `"rank"`, `"dens"`, `"pairs"` or
`"energy"`, and `vignette("diagnostics")` shows a trace plot. For
anything else, pass the draws and the sampler's quantities to bayesplot
yourself:

```{r bayesplot, eval = FALSE}
bayesplot::mcmc_areas(firms$draws, pars = c("mean_g", "sd_g"))
bayesplot::mcmc_nuts_divergence(bayesplot::nuts_params(firms),
                                bayesplot::log_posterior(firms))
```

Note that the stored fits are thinned to 1 draw in 15, so their trace
plots show 200 draws for each chain, whereas the sampler diagnostics in
`plot_diagnostics()` are computed from the whole run. The energy plot
compares each iteration with the one before it and is available only for
a fit that stores every iteration. See `vignette("diagnostics")` for the
call.
